title: Remove Linked List Elements
description: Brute force to optimized: filtering values and rebuilding versus a dummy head that uniformly handles removing even a matching true head.

blocks.text: Given the head of a singly linked list and an integer val, remove ALL nodes whose value equals val, and return the new head.

blocks.caption: A dummy head handles the case where even the real head needs removing, uniformly with every other node

blocks.text: Given a linked list and a target value, remove every single node holding that value, wherever it appears in the list, including possibly the very first node.

blocks.title: Analogy: Removing Every Occurrence of a Specific Name From a Guest List
blocks.text: Like walking down a guest list crossing out every entry for a specific person's name, wherever it appears, even if that name happens to be the very first entry on the list. Using a blank "placeholder" line before the list even starts makes crossing out the first real entry exactly as easy as crossing out any entry in the middle, with no special first-entry handling needed at all.

blocks.caption: The dummy head lets every node, including the first, be checked and removed identically

blocks.text: Before worrying about special-casing whether the very first node itself needs removing, notice that a placeholder "dummy" node placed just before the real head makes every single node in the list, including the first, follow the exact same removal logic.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Removing a node in the MIDDLE of a list is easy: just redirect the PRECEDING node's next pointer to skip over it.

Observation 2: Removing the very FIRST node (the head) is normally awkward, since there's no preceding node to redirect; a completely different line of code would otherwise be needed just for that one special case.

Observation 3: Introducing a dummy node, placed immediately before the real head, gives EVERY node (including the true first one) a "preceding node" to work with, unifying the removal logic into one single, uniform case.

Observation 4: Walking forward with a curr pointer (starting at the dummy), checking curr.next's value at each step: if it matches val, skip it directly (curr.next = curr.next.next, without advancing curr, to catch consecutive matches); otherwise, advance curr forward past the confirmed non-match.

Recognizing that a dummy head eliminates the need for separate first-node-removal logic is a broadly useful simplification whenever a linked list operation might need to remove or modify the very first node.

This is the dummy head technique, a broadly reusable simplification for any linked list problem where the head itself might need to be modified or removed, unifying that case with every other node's handling.
Filter out every matching value into a plain array, then rebuild an entirely new linked list from the filtered values.

items: Walk through the original list, collecting only the values that do NOT match val into an array.
Build a brand new linked list from this filtered array of values.

codes.python:
def remove_elements(head, val):
    values = []
    node = head
    while node:
        if node.val != val:
            values.append(node.val)                                       # keep only values that don't match
        node = node.next
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    cur = dummy
    for v in values:
        cur.next = ListNode(v)                                             # rebuild a brand new list from the filtered values
        cur = cur.next
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(6, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5, ListNode(6)))))))
    result = remove_elements(head, 6)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Values are filtered directly during the first pass, since only non-matching values need to survive into the final list.
A brand new linked list is built from the filtered values, since this brute force does not reuse any of the original nodes.
The dummy head simplifies building the NEW list, though it doesn't address the original list's head-removal problem directly (since the whole list is rebuilt anyway).

blocks.text: Every matching value is correctly filtered out, so the resulting list is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to filter plus one pass to rebuild.
Space: O(n), for the intermediate array and the entirely new set of nodes created.
Limitation: creating brand new nodes ignores that the EXISTING nodes can simply be re-linked in place, skipping over matching ones directly, achieving the same result with O(1) extra space.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force creates entirely new nodes. Instead, introduce a dummy node pointing to the real head, and maintain a curr pointer starting at dummy. At each step, check curr.next's value: if it matches val, skip it directly by setting curr.next = curr.next.next (without moving curr, to catch any immediately following match too); otherwise, advance curr to curr.next. This uniformly handles removing the true head just like any other matching node.

Create dummy pointing to head, and set curr to dummy. While curr.next is not null: if curr.next.val equals val, set curr.next = curr.next.next (skip the match); otherwise, advance curr to curr.next. Return dummy.next once the loop ends.
Use a dummy head so every node, including a matching true head, is removed using the exact same uniform logic.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass through the list.
Space: O(1) extra, reusing the existing nodes and only the dummy plus a single curr pointer.

The dummy node gives every node in the ORIGINAL list, including the true head, a valid "preceding node" (dummy itself, or some node reached via dummy) whose next pointer can be redirected. curr only ever advances past a node CONFIRMED not to match val; when a match is found, curr.next is redirected to skip it, and curr deliberately stays in place, since the node that slides into curr.next's position might ALSO match val (handling consecutive matches correctly without any extra logic).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["curr.next.val == val","Skip curr.next directly (curr.next = curr.next.next); curr stays in place to re-check the new next node"],["curr.next.val != val","Advance curr forward to curr.next, since this node is confirmed to stay in the list"]]}

items: dummy.next is initialized to the real head, so the dummy node correctly represents "the node before the list begins".
curr starts at dummy (not head), ensuring even a matching true head is handled by the same uniform logic as every other node.
The function returns dummy.next at the end, which correctly reflects the new head, whether or not the original head was removed.

blocks.text: The dummy head technique is a broadly reusable simplification whenever a linked list operation might need to remove or modify the very first node, since it gives every node (including the true head) a uniform "preceding node" to work with.

items: Forgetting to advance curr only after confirming a non-match, which would incorrectly skip past a SECOND consecutive matching node without removing it.
Not using a dummy head, forcing separate special-case logic for the specific scenario where the true head itself needs removing.
Returning head instead of dummy.next at the end, which would incorrectly return the ORIGINAL head even if it had already been removed.

items: Explicitly justify the dummy head's purpose (uniformly handling a potentially-removed true head), since this is a broadly transferable technique interviewers want to see recognized and applied correctly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Remove all nodes matching some condition, INCLUDING possibly the head itself" points toward the dummy head technique, unifying the head-removal case with every other node's handling.

items: How would you solve this recursively instead? Recursively process the rest of the list first, then decide whether to include the current node based on whether its value matches val, naturally handling removal at any position including the head.

How would you remove nodes matching any value from a given SET of values, not just one? The exact same technique applies directly, just checking curr.next.val against set membership instead of a single equality check.

What if you needed to remove nodes based on their POSITION rather than their value (e.g., every 3rd node)? The same dummy-head-plus-skip technique still applies, just tracking a position counter instead of checking values.
The dummy head technique, a broadly reusable simplification also seen in Merge Two Sorted Lists and applicable to many other linked list problems where the head itself might need modification.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (dummy head, in-place skip): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Dummy head technique, unifying head-node removal with every other node's removal logic
Core Idea: A placeholder node before the true head lets every node, including the head, be checked and removed using identical logic
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: A dummy head eliminates the need for separate special-case logic whenever a linked list's true head might need to be removed or modified
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Dummy head; if curr.next.val == val skip it (stay put), else advance curr
